bullets.title: Sum: Forty Tales from the Afterlives
bullets.creator: Stanford neuroscientist David Eagleman
bullets.note: fourhourmail.com/c/mvu8n09oou5hmnqggsq/g7hnh5ho8dr07w/aHR0cHM6Ly90d2l0dGVyLmNvbS9kYXZpZGVhZ2xlbWFu)). Don’t let the title of this book fool you; it isn’t making a case for the afterlife. Instead, this short read (easy to finish in 1–2 days) is a collection of 40 thought exercises on the nature of existence, reality, perception, death, pain, boredom, and more. It’s remarkably elegant and fun. At the very least, it should make you appreciate your own life—warts and all—much more. From the book’s official description: “In one afterlife, you may find that God is the size of a microbe and unaware of your existence. In another version, you work as a background character in other people’s dreams. Or you may find that God is a married couple, or that the universe is running backward, or that you are forced to live out your afterlife with annoying versions of who you could have been.”
